stem:
Rudo determines the relative formula mass of a Group 2 carbonate, $\ce{MCO3}$, by heating it until it has fully decomposed:

$\ce{MCO3(s) -> MO(s) + CO2(g)}$

For each experiment she weighs an empty crucible, adds the carbonate and weighs again, then heats the crucible strongly with a Bunsen burner, lets it cool on a heat-resistant mat with the lid on, and reweighs. She repeats the heating, cooling and weighing until two consecutive masses agree (constant mass). In experiment 4 she ran out of time and heated the crucible only once. The balance reads to 0.01 g and each reading has an uncertainty of ±0.005 g.

| Experiment | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mass of empty crucible / g | 15.62 | 16.08 | 15.87 | 16.31 | 15.94 |
| Mass of crucible + carbonate / g | 16.64 | 17.59 | 17.89 | 18.80 | 18.97 |
| Mass of crucible + residue after heating / g | 16.11 | 16.80 | 16.84 | 17.85 | 17.39 |

Use Mr of $\ce{CO2}$ = 44.0, Ar: C 12.0, O 16.0.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of carbonate used, in g, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide lost, in g, to two decimal places.
parts.explanation: 17.89 − 16.84 = 1.05 g. (0.97 g is the mass of the residue, not the gas lost.)
parts.workedSolution: 1. 17.89 − 16.84 = 1.05 g. (0.97 g is the mass of the residue, not the gas lost.)

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why Rudo heats to constant mass, and why the crucible is cooled with its lid on before each weighing.

points.description: Constant mass shows that decomposition is complete, so all the CO₂ has been lost
Weighing hot gives a false (low) reading because of convection currents / the lid stops the oxide absorbing water vapour or CO₂ from the air (and stops solid spitting out)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Two equal consecutive masses show that no more carbon dioxide is being lost, so the decomposition is complete. The crucible is cooled before weighing because convection currents above a hot crucible make the reading unreliable, and the lid stops the oxide absorbing moisture or carbon dioxide from the air while it cools.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which experiment number gives the anomalous result?
parts.explanation: Experiment 4 lost only 0.95 g of CO₂ from 2.49 g; about 1.30 g was expected from the line through the other points. It was heated only once, so decomposition was incomplete.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Rudo plots mass of carbon dioxide lost against mass of carbonate. Describe the graph she should draw.

points.description: Mass of CO₂ lost / g on the y-axis against mass of carbonate / g on the x-axis, labelled with units, scales using more than half the grid in each direction
A straight line of best fit passing through the origin, ignoring the anomalous point (experiment 4)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Plot mass of carbon dioxide lost / g (y) against mass of carbonate / g (x), with scales chosen so the points fill more than half of the grid, then draw a straight best-fit line through the origin that ignores experiment 4.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Determine the gradient of the best-fit line through the origin (no unit; exclude the anomaly).
parts.explanation: Line through the origin fitted to experiments 1, 2, 3 and 5: gradient ≈ 0.521 (for example 1.58 ÷ 3.03 = 0.521). Any value from 0.511 to 0.531 is accepted.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Line through the origin fitted to experiments 1, 2, 3 and 5: gradient ≈ 0.521 (for example 1.58 ÷ 3.03 = 0.521). Any value from 0.511 to 0.531 is accepted.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Use your gradient to calculate the relative formula mass of MCO₃.
parts.explanation: 1 mol MCO₃ (Mr g) loses 1 mol CO₂ (44.0 g), so mass lost = (44.0 ÷ Mr) × mass of carbonate and the gradient = 44.0 ÷ Mr. Mr = 44.0 ÷ 0.521 = 84.4. Multiplying instead of dividing gives a meaningless 22.9.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 1 mol MCO₃ (Mr g) loses 1 mol CO₂ (44.0 g), so mass lost = (44.0 ÷ Mr) × mass of carbonate and the gradient = 44.0 ÷ Mr. Mr = 44.0 ÷ 0.521 = 84.4. Multiplying instead of dividing gives a meaningless 22.9.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the relative atomic mass of M.
parts.explanation: Ar(M) = 84.4 − (12.0 + 3 × 16.0) = 24.4. Subtracting 44.0 (CO₂) instead of 60.0 (CO₃) is a common slip.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Ar(M) = 84.4 − (12.0 + 3 × 16.0) = 24.4. Subtracting 44.0 (CO₂) instead of 60.0 (CO₃) is a common slip.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.explanation: Ar ≈ 24: magnesium (Ar 24.3). Calcium (40.1) would give Mr ≈ 100.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of carbon dioxide lost in experiment 1, to two significant figures.
parts.explanation: The mass lost is a difference of two readings, so the uncertainty is 2 × 0.005 = 0.01 g; 0.01 ÷ 0.53 × 100 = 1.9%. Using ±0.005 g once gives 0.94%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The mass lost is a difference of two readings, so the uncertainty is 2 × 0.005 = 0.01 g; 0.01 ÷ 0.53 × 100 = 1.9%. Using ±0.005 g once gives 0.94%.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Explain the effect on the calculated Mr if every sample had been heated only once, as in experiment 4.

points.description: Less CO₂ is lost than the full amount, so the gradient (mass lost ÷ mass of carbonate) is smaller
Mr = 44.0 ÷ gradient, so the calculated Mr is too high

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Incomplete decomposition means less carbon dioxide is lost from each sample, so the gradient is smaller. Since Mr = 44.0 ÷ gradient, the calculated Mr would be too high.

parts.label: (j)
parts.stem: Identify one systematic error and one random error in this method, and state the direction of the effect of the systematic error on Mr.

points.description: Systematic: e.g. the oxide absorbs water/CO₂ from the air while cooling, or solid is lost by spitting, or the carbonate is damp / partly basic carbonate
Direction consistent with the error: absorption gives a smaller mass loss so Mr too high; spitting or a damp sample gives a larger mass loss so Mr too low
Random: e.g. reading the balance / small differences in heating and cooling time between experiments / variation in the amount of solid lost from the crucible

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A systematic error is the oxide absorbing moisture from the air as it cools: every residue weighs a little too much, the mass lost is too small, the gradient is too small and Mr too high. A random error is the variation in heating and cooling times from one experiment to another, which scatters the points about the line.

parts.label: (k)
parts.stem: Suggest three improvements to the method.

points.description: Heat every sample to constant mass (repeat heating until two readings agree), including experiment 4
Cool in a desiccator before weighing to stop the oxide absorbing moisture
Use a balance reading to 0.001 g or larger masses of carbonate to reduce the percentage uncertainty; repeat experiments / use more data points

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Repeat experiment 4, heating to constant mass; cool each crucible in a desiccator so the oxide cannot absorb water from the air; and use a balance reading to 0.001 g (or larger samples) to reduce the percentage uncertainty in the small mass losses.

parts.label: (l)
parts.stem: Rudo's friend suggests repeating the experiment with barium carbonate. Suggest why this method would not work well, and state one safety precaution for the original experiment.

points.description: Thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group, so barium carbonate does not decompose (or decomposes only very slowly) at Bunsen temperature
Wear eye protection / use tongs and a heat-resistant mat for the hot crucible / keep the lid partly on to avoid spitting solid

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Group 2 carbonates become more thermally stable down the group, so barium carbonate would hardly decompose at the temperature of a Bunsen flame. Wear eye protection and handle the hot crucible with tongs.

explanation: Gradient ≈ 0.521; Mr(MCO₃) ≈ 84.4; Ar(M) ≈ 24.4, so M is magnesium. Experiment 4 is anomalous (heated only once).
hints: A mass found by difference has twice the uncertainty of one reading.
